ety.text: From light(e)n + -ing. Doublet of lightening.

senses.d: A flash of light produced by short-duration, high-voltage discharge of electricity within a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the earth.
ex: Although we did not see the lightning, we did hear the thunder.
Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go, and say unto thee, Here we are?

senses.d: A discharge of this kind.
ex: The lightning was hot enough to melt the sand.
That tree was hit by lightning.

senses.d: Anything that moves very fast.
Gin.
Extremely fast or sudden; moving (as if) at the speed of lightning.
ex: The insurgents then began their lightning advance along the Euphrates in the Sunni heartland toward Baghdad.

senses.d: To produce lightning.
ex: "Hey!" yelled Reggie, pulling her back. "Get in here! It's lightninging. I don't want a charcoal-broiled friend!"

Inherited from Old French foudre, from Latin fulgura, nominative plural of fulgur, from Proto-Italic *folgos. Alternatively, from fulgere.

Cognate with Saterland Frisian ljoacht (“light”), Dutch licht, German licht.

From Middle English liȝt, lyghte, from Old English lēht, lēoht, līht, from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz or *līhtaz (“light (in weight)”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“lightweight”).
From Middle English lighten, from Old English līhtan (“to relieve”), from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄htijan, from Proto-Germanic *linhtijaną, from *linhtaz (“light”).

senses.d: Electromagnetic radiation in the wavelength range visible to the human eye (about 400–750 nanometers): visible light.
ex: As you can see, this spacious dining-room gets a lot of light in the mornings.
When the studio light is on, I am recording my evening show.

senses.d: Electromagnetic radiation in the wavelength range visible to the human eye or in nearby ranges (infrared or ultraviolet radiation).
ex: black light

senses.d: Electromagnetic radiation of any wavelength.
A source of illumination.
ex: Put that light out!
And the light ſhineth in darkneſſe, and the darkneſſe compꝛehended it not.

senses.d: A lightbulb or similar light-emitting device, regardless of whether it is lit.
ex: We turned off all the lights and went to sleep.

senses.d: A traffic light, or (by extension) an intersection controlled by traffic lights.
ex: To get to our house, turn right at the third light.

senses.d: Spiritual or mental illumination; enlightenment, useful information.
ex: Can you throw any light on this problem?
He shall never know / That I had any light of this from thee.

senses.d: Facts; pieces of information; ideas, concepts.
ex: Now these notions are twofold, actions or habits[…], which are durable lights and notions, which we may use when we will.
"Well, there's her statement of her case, and according to her lights, it's a just one. She's got a slum-bred mind."

senses.d: A notable person within a specific field or discipline.
ex: Picasso was one of the leading lights of the cubist movement.
Joan of Arc, a light of ancient France

senses.d: The manner in which the light strikes a picture; that part of a picture which represents those objects upon which the light is supposed to fall; the more illuminated part of a landscape or other scene; opposed to shade.
To start (a fire).
ex: We lit the fire to get some heat.

senses.d: To set fire to; to set burning.
ex: She lit her last match.
if a thousand candles be all lighted from one

senses.d: To illuminate; to provide light for when it is dark.
ex: I used my torch to light the way home through the woods in the night.
The Sun has set, and Vesper, to supply / His absent beams, had lighted up the sky.

senses.d: To become ignited; to take fire.
ex: This soggy match will not light.

senses.d: To attend or conduct with a light; to show the way to by means of a light.
ex: His bishops lead him forth, and light him on.

senses.d: To make (a bonus) available to be collected by hitting a target, and thus light up the feature light corresponding to that bonus to indicate its availability.
ex: Light the extra ball by amassing 500 million points in the wizard mode.

senses.d: Having light; bright; clear; not dark or obscure.
ex: The room is light when the Sun shines through the window.

senses.d: Pale or whitish in color; highly luminous and more or less deficient in chroma.
ex: She had light skin.

senses.d: Served with extra milk or cream.
ex: Do you want your coffee light or black? -I like mine light.

senses.d: Having little or relatively little actual weight; not heavy; not cumbrous or unwieldy.
ex: a light load ; a lighter backpack after having removed the books ; light weapons

senses.d: Having little weight as compared with bulk; of little density or specific gravity.
ex: feathers and cork are light ; oil is lighter than water

senses.d: Of short or insufficient weight; weighing less than the legal, standard, or proper amount; clipped or diminished.
ex: to issue light coin

senses.d: Free from burden or impediment; unencumbered.
Lightly built; typically designed for speed or small loads.
ex: a light aircraft ; a light tank

senses.d: Not heavily armed; armed with light weapons.
ex: light infantry; a troop of light horse

senses.d: Riding high because of no cargo; by extension, pertaining to a ship which is light.
ex: if a ship is light or partially loaded ; the light draft of a vessel, or its light displacement

senses.d: Without any piece of equipment attached or attached only to a caboose.
ex: the light locomotives ; a locomotive may be moved light

senses.d: With low viscosity.
Not heavy or soggy; spongy; well raised.
ex: a light bread ; sponge cake is a light cake

senses.d: Carrying little.
ex: I prefer to travel light.

senses.d: A stone that is not thrown hard enough.
See lights (“lungs”).
A low-alcohol lager.
ex: We crossed to the pub on the corner of Carlisle Street and I ordered two schooners of old for him and one of light for me.

senses.d: A member of the light cavalry.
To unload a ship, or to jettison material to make it lighter.
To lighten; to ease of a burden; to take off.
ex: His mailèd habergeon she did undight, / And from his head his heavy burgonet did light.

senses.d: To leave; to depart.
To find by chance.
ex: I lit upon a rare book in a second-hand bookseller's.

senses.d: To stop upon (of eyes or a glance); to notice.
ex: "Sacredam!" he cried, when his eyes lit upon Buck. "Dat one dam bully dog! Eh? How moch?"

senses.d: To alight; to land or come down.
ex: She fell out of the window but luckily lit on her feet.
And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel.

From Middle English lightere, lyghtere, equivalent to light (“to unload, lighten”) + -er. Compare West Frisian lichter (“lighter ship”), Dutch lichter (“lighter ship”), Middle Low German lichter, lüchter, lüchtære (“a small ship that lightens a load, lighter ship”).

senses.d: A person who lights things.
ex: a lighter of lamps

senses.d: A device used to light things, especially a reusable handheld device for creating fire to light cigarettes.
ex: Cigarette in mouth, he clutched his pockets in search of a lighter.

senses.d: A flat-bottomed boat for carrying heavy loads across short distances (especially for canals or for loading or unloading larger boats).
To transfer (cargo or passengers) to or from a ship by means of a lighter or other small vessel.
To transfer cargo or fuel from (a ship), lightening it to make its draft less or to make it easier to refloat.
